source.title: Comparative performance of large language models in emotional safety classification across sizes and tasks
source.authors: Edoardo Pinzuti; O. Tüscher; André Ferreira Castro

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some tables are flattened in the supplied text; unclear table values were not assigned to models.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream classification performance across model sizes, rather than measuring pretraining loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports emotional-safety classification outcomes, which bear on V6. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, power-law fits or extrapolations, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or architecture-shape comparisons. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. The text mentions a BERT comparison, but it is not a model-size scaling result.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream safety-classification accuracy across four LLaMA 3 sizes (1B–70B) under fixed prompting regimes. This bears on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6) in a new task setting. It fits no scaling law and reports no pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that larger LLaMA models perform better, especially zero-shot and on multi-label taxonomy. Few-shot prompting narrows the gap (most strongly in the trinary task), and LoRA fine-tuning lets a 1B model match the 70B model and BERT on high-data categories. They conclude performance is not solely a function of scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares downstream emotional-safety classification accuracy across model sizes and supervision settings; it does not reproduce pretraining-loss scaling measurements or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Classification outcomes vary with zero-shot versus few-shot prompting, fine-tuning, and taxonomy category. The authors report non-monotonic category-level scaling and note that the full six-category evaluation used single runs.

fits_no_version.finding: A LoRA-fine-tuned 1B model reaches 0.86 mean accuracy on three high-data categories, versus 0.835 for 70B FS-5, and exceeds 3B/8B FS-5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-specific fine-tuning of a small model can match or beat much larger prompted models on a downstream classification task.

record.problems: The paper evaluates classification accuracy rather than held-out pretraining loss. The full six-category evaluation was based on single runs, some categories were underrepresented, and the supplied table text is flattened, limiting reliable assignment of some values. The dataset includes LLM-generated variants, which the authors say may introduce stylistic artifacts.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported values were omitted where they could be assigned reliably from the supplied text. Individual Table 2 and some Table 3 entries were not extracted because the flattened table layout does not reliably associate values with models and conditions. BERT comparator values were left out because they do not provide a model-size scaling result.

untested.parts: All of it: no pretraining loss is measured.
All of it. Fine-tuning is used, but no power law is fitted.
Predictability from pretraining loss. Any quantitative fit of accuracy against scale.

missing.what: Per-size FS-5 and ZS-5 mean accuracies (1B, 3B, 8B, 70B) on high-data categories, and the FS-5 scaling line against VRAM
Per-size trinary accuracies (zero-shot and few-shot). Flattened values suggest non-monotonic ordering between 3B and 8B.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is weak for V6. There are only four model sizes from different LLaMA releases (3.2/3.1/3.3), all instruct-tuned and 4-bit quantized. No trend is fitted. The full taxonomy was evaluated as a single run with 30 posts per class, and the dataset is partly LLM-generated. The mean values in the flattened Table 3 (e.g. 0.208 vs the 0.176 given in the text for 1B FS-1) may conflict with the text.

Prediction of larger-run pretraining loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.

relationships.condition: Mean accuracy across LLaMA 3 sizes 1B–70B, zero-shot and few-shot, taxonomy task (plus Qwen per the authors)
relationships.reason: Mean taxonomy accuracy rises monotonically 1B→70B under both ZS-1 and FS-1 (r1, r2). The authors state the trend is robust over five runs (r14) and is replicated in Qwen (r16).
relationships.display_finding: Mean taxonomy accuracy increases monotonically from 1B to 70B in zero-shot and few-shot settings, with the trend robust across five runs and replicated in Qwen.

relationships.condition: Individual harm categories; trinary task under few-shot prompting
relationships.reason: The authors report non-monotonic category-level scaling, e.g. 3B beating 8B, and call it real rather than noise (r15). Few-shot prompting largely closes the size gap on the trinary task (r4).
relationships.display_finding: The 3B model sometimes outperformed 8B across harm categories, while few-shot prompting largely closed the trinary classification gap.
